newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German supertrain has edge, but future uncertain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German supertrain has edge, but future uncertain.

text.p: The sleek Transrapid magnetic levitation train leaves a vapour trail as it rushes past close to its top speed of 420 km (260 miles) an hour, but it makes less noise than a farmer's tractor chugging by.

The train of the future, which has no screeching wheels or conventional rails, floats on a magnetic cushion one centimetre above the 32 km (20 miles) test track in this out-of-the-way corner of northern Germany.

With a tongue-and-groove construction that keeps it from flying off the track, the Transrapid feels to passengers more like an aircraft as it banks steeply into a curve. It has a comfortable lead over its only comparable competitor, Japan's "linear motor car".
But the prestige project faces popular opposition at home and a lack of clear markets. The planners' efforts to push the Transrapid toward the silence barrier are part of a plan to quiet the critics.

"We've tried to think not only of the passengers but of the people in the surrounding area, by minimising noise and vibration," said Guenter Steinmetz, chief engineer at the test track, which has been in operation since 1984.
"If people aren't disturbed by the train, they will have nothing to complain about," Steinmetz told journalists after a test ride.
HAMBURG TO BERLIN

The first commercial Transrapid line is planned for the 290 km (180 miles) Hamburg-Berlin route, an opportunity opened by German unification in 1990. Construction is due to start in 1998 and operations in 2005.

"We have the plan that makes the most sense for the environment, for transportation, and for business," said Hans Christoph Atzpodien, president of the Magnetschnellbahn Plannungsgesellschaft GmbH, planners of the German train.

The government has committed 5.6 billion marks ($3.58 billion) for the Hamburg-Berlin track. The total cost is conservatively seen at nine billion, with the rest underwritten by a group comprising Thyssen Industrie AG, Siemens AG, ADtranz, Hochtief AG, Philipp Holzmann AG, Bilfinger & Berger Bau AG and Deutsche Bahn AG.
Lufthansa AG and Deutsche Bahn each have a 50 percent share in the company running the test track.

Private and public sector officials believe the Transrapid, connecting downtown Hamburg to downtown Berlin in under an hour, will make air traffic on the route superfluous, and also lure a large number of passengers from the motorway.

But opponents, mainly environmentalists and elected officials in the state of Schleswig-Holstein that surrounds Hamburg, are doing their utmost to block the project, which they say is unnecessary, unrealistic and overpriced.
To avert conflict, the planners have tried to lay much of the route along existing railways, roads and power lines, but affected landowners are protesting. The final route has not been decided.
LOOKING BEYOND BORDERS

The planners say the Hamburg-Berlin route would be economically viable on its own, but they are already thinking beyond. Having a working Transrapid line in Germany is a key ingredient in their plans to export the train.
The Netherlands is talking about extending the route to Amsterdam, and preliminary plans are being made to extend the route south from Berlin to Dresden and eventually on to Prague.
Atzpodien said large-scale rail projects for which the Transrapid might be appropriate are also in planning in the United States, South America, East Asia and Australia.

Still, the success of the Transrapid will depend on its integration into the "Trans-European Network". But that European Union-sponsored megaproject appears to be losing budgetary steam in the cost-slashing run-up to monetary union.

And it emphasises the previous generation of conventional high-speed trains the top speeds of which are in the 250-300 kph (155-186 mph) range, represented by France's TGV and Germany's ICE, with no clear plans to develop the Transrapid beyond the Hamburg-Berlin link. EU funds would require the assent of France, which is zealously promoting its TGV.
BEATING THE JAPANESE
For at least some of these export projects, the German train may have Japan's "linear motor car" to contend with.

"The Transrapid is technically the superior system, and we have more experience," Atzpodien said. "But we cannot afford to be complacent. Japan will certainly pursue its project energetically once it is under way."

The Japanese developers have had a seven-km (four-mile) test track in operation since the 1970s, but they are now building a 40-km (25-mile) track, part of which is set to be running next April. The new test track will be integrated in the heavily travelled Tokyo-Osaka route if and when that is realised.
The Japanese train has a maximum speed of more than 500 km (310 miles) an hour, reducing the Tokyo-Osaka trip to one hour, less than the average commute from the Tokyo suburbs to the city centre.

The German developers are putting great stress on beating the Japanese to the market. They believe Germany's conventional high-speed ICE is technologically superior to France's TGV, but that France has been more successful in marketing the TGV, winning major projects in South Korea and the U.S. because the French system was on the market earlier.
"I have the feeling the Germans are thinking a great deal about Japan, but we are not thinking so much about them, or about exports," said Kozo Fujita, a transport official at the Japanese embassy.

Fujita conceded that the German project is further developed than the Japanese which he said was being built with the domestic market in mind. The Tokyo-Osaka route at the trunk of the system already carries seven times as many passengers a year as the 14.5 million Germany hopes to build on the Hamburg-Berlin route, a figure German critics say is wildly optimistic.
Fujita said there was no way of knowing how long it would take to build the maglev track in Japan once the political decision is made, as Japan has citizens' movements of its own.
Tokyo's Narita International Airport took 30 years to build because of opposition from student radicals and local farmers, he noted.

The German and Japanese maglev systems are technologically incompatible, with the Japanese train relying on superconducting magnets. Designed for an earthquake-prone country, it needs conventional wheels at speeds below 100 km (62 miles) an hour. ($1=1.5647 Mark)
